title: Estimating the size of a nucleus
body: In the Geiger-Marsden experiment, a collimated beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source fell on a very thin gold foil, and the scattered particles were counted with a rotatable zinc sulphide screen and microscope. For a head-on collision, an alpha particle (charge 2e) slows down as it approaches the nucleus (charge Ze), stops momentarily and turns back. Since the total mechanical energy of the alpha particle and nucleus is conserved, the initial kinetic energy K equals the electric potential energy at the stopping point. This gives the distance of closest approach d = 2Ze^2/(4 pi epsilon_0 K). The nucleus is taken to be at rest because it is much heavier than the alpha particle. A student first uses alpha particles of kinetic energy K on gold (Z = 79) and records the distance of closest approach as d. She then plans a second run with a silver foil (Z = 47) and alpha particles of kinetic energy 2K.

title: Exciting hydrogen gas by electron collisions
body: The energy of a hydrogen atom in its nth stationary state is E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The first few values are E_1 = -13.6 eV, E_2 = -3.40 eV, E_3 = -1.51 eV and E_4 = -0.85 eV. At room temperature almost all atoms in hydrogen gas are in the ground state. In a laboratory, a beam of electrons is fired into hydrogen gas at room temperature. In a collision, an electron of the beam can give part or all of its kinetic energy to an atom, but the atom accepts energy only in amounts that take it exactly to one of its allowed higher levels. An excited atom then returns to lower levels, either directly or in steps, emitting a photon at each jump. The light from the tube is analysed with a spectrometer. In one run every electron in the beam has a kinetic energy of 12.5 eV.
